---
title: "Agent Harness"
---

## 1. What Is a Harness?

A foundation model maps context to tokens or structured actions. By itself, it
does not own a durable workspace, execute tools, preserve state across context
windows, enforce permissions, recover from failures, or decide when external
work is complete.

An **agent harness** is the software system surrounding the model that supplies
those capabilities. It determines how the model:

- receives goals, rules, context, and observations
- selects and invokes tools
- iterates through a workflow
- stores state and artifacts
- delegates or monitors background work
- verifies progress and completion
- interacts with users at permission or clarification boundaries

Lilian Weng describes the harness as the deployment layer that orchestrates how
the model thinks and plans, acts through tools, perceives and manages context,
stores artifacts, and evaluates results. Her
[Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement](https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2026-07-04-harness/)
is the main reference for this note.

A useful decomposition is

$$
\boxed{
\text{agent system}
=
\text{model}
+
\text{harness}
+
\text{environment}
}.
$$

The model supplies learned reasoning and generation. The harness supplies the
runtime contract. The environment supplies files, applications, APIs, people,
and consequences.

## 2. What a Harness Is Not

| Concept | Role |
|---|---|
| Foundation model | predicts text, decisions, or tool calls from context |
| Agent harness | turns model decisions into a controlled, stateful execution process |
| Agent framework | library used to build harnesses; it is not the configured system itself |
| Workflow | one control policy or graph implemented by the harness |
| Tool | a bounded capability exposed through the harness |
| Evaluation harness | runs tasks and computes measurements about a system |

An evaluation harness **measures** behavior. An agent harness **produces and
controls** behavior. An agent harness may call verifiers during execution, but
that does not make it merely an evaluation framework.

The word “scaffold” is sometimes used similarly. “Harness” emphasizes the whole
runtime boundary: execution, context, memory, permissions, observability, and
workflow—not just a prompt template.

## 3. The First-Principles Problem

The harness exists because a model call is stateless and probabilistic, while a
real task is stateful and governed by constraints.

Let $M$ be a model, $H$ a harness, $e$ an environment, and $x$ a task. We care
about system behavior

$$
\tau\sim P(\tau\mid M,H,e,x),
$$

where trajectory $\tau$ contains model decisions, tool calls, observations,
state changes, and the final result. Harness design seeks to maximize expected
utility:

$$
H^*
=
\arg\max_H
\mathbb E_{\tau}
\left[
R_{\text{task}}(\tau)
-\lambda_c C(\tau)
-\lambda_t T(\tau)
-\lambda_r R_{\text{risk}}(\tau)
\right].
$$

This framing yields several important insights:

1. Model quality and harness quality are confounded in end-to-end results.
2. More autonomy is not inherently better; it is useful only where adaptive
   decisions outperform deterministic code.
3. Reliability must come from system invariants, not from hoping the model
   remembers every rule on every turn.
4. The harness should make success observable and failure recoverable.

### From predictor to closed-loop decision system

A model call is an open-loop predictor: it maps its current context to a proposed
continuation or action. A harness turns repeated calls into feedback control:

$$
s_t
\xrightarrow{\text{predict and decide}}
a_t
\xrightarrow{\text{environment}}
o_{t+1}
\xrightarrow{\text{compare}}
\delta_t
\xrightarrow{\text{update}}
s_{t+1},
$$

where $s_t$ is the harness's current state estimate, $o_{t+1}$ is an external
observation, and $\delta_t$ is the mismatch between expected and observed
consequences. This is more precise than simply saying that an LLM “becomes an
agent”:

$$
\boxed{\text{open-loop predictor}\rightarrow\text{closed-loop decision system}}.
$$

Most harness mechanisms can be located within this loop:

| Decision-loop problem | Harness mechanism | Control role |
|---|---|---|
| What is currently true? | context, retrieval, memory, task state | state estimation |
| What might happen? | reasoning, planning, candidate generation | consequence prediction |
| What should happen next? | controller, routing, skills | action selection and abstraction |
| How can the system intervene or learn? | tools | actuation and sensing |
| Did reality disagree? | tests, verifiers, critics | surprise generation |
| Which assumption failed? | diagnosis and reflection | error attribution |
| What must survive? | artifacts, checkpoints, persistent memory | state update |
| Where may the agent go? | permissions and guardrails | reachable-state constraints |
| How does the system improve? | traces, evaluations, failure analysis | outer-loop learning |

This view asks what information closes the loop. Adding more internal reasoning
cannot correct a false belief as reliably as an environmental observation that
distinguishes competing hypotheses.

## 4. The Basic Agent Loop

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    G[Goal and constraints] --> C[Compile current context]
    C --> M[Model decision]
    M --> D{Decision type}
    D -- Tool call --> P[Validate permissions and arguments]
    P --> X[Execute tool]
    X --> O[Normalize and record observation]
    O --> S[Update state and artifacts]
    S --> V[Check progress, limits, and failures]
    V -- Continue --> C
    D -- Candidate answer --> F[Verify completion conditions]
    F -- Incomplete --> S
    F -- Complete --> A[Return result]
    V -- Needs authority or clarification --> U[Ask user]
    U --> S
```

The model does not call the operating system or an API directly. It proposes an
action; the harness validates, authorizes, executes, records, and returns a
bounded observation. That indirection is the key control boundary.

OpenAI's open-source Codex runtime is a concrete implementation of this loop.
See [Codex: Anatomy of an Open-Source Coding Agent](codex.qmd) for a source-level
analysis of its turn loop, typed tool router, event protocol, persistence, and
sandbox boundary.

### Model decisions versus code decisions

Use the model when the choice requires semantic judgment under ambiguity. Use
ordinary code when the rule is known:

| Better handled by the model | Better handled by the harness |
|---|---|
| choosing a promising hypothesis | enforcing a maximum tool-call count |
| deciding what evidence is missing | validating JSON against a schema |
| interpreting an unfamiliar error | applying timeouts and retry limits |
| proposing a plan revision | checking an exit code |
| synthesizing several observations | requiring approval for a destructive action |

Encoding deterministic invariants as prose wastes model capacity and makes
them probabilistic.

## 5. Harness Components {#sec-harness-components}

### 5.1 Context compiler

The context compiler decides what the model sees on the next turn. It assembles:

1. immutable system and safety rules
2. task contract and user instructions
3. available tool interfaces
4. active plan and working state
5. relevant persistent memory and artifacts
6. recent observations and errors

It must resolve ordering, priority, truncation, compaction, and provenance.
Simply appending every prior token eventually produces an expensive, noisy, and
contradictory context.

Context layout also affects inference cost. A stable prompt prefix can reuse
cached transformer computation, whereas reordering tools or rewriting old
messages can invalidate that cache. Codex consequently treats model-visible
history as append-oriented state, orders dynamic inputs deterministically, and
represents environment or permission changes as new context items when possible.
This suggests a further invariant:

> Keep stable context stable. Compile semantic changes without gratuitously
> perturbing the reusable prefix.

In control terms, context and memory perform **state estimation**. From the full
history

$$
h_t=(o_1,a_1,\ldots,o_t),
$$

the harness constructs a compact state $s_t=\phi(h_t)$ that should preserve the
information needed for future decisions:

$$
p(o_{t+1}\mid h_t,a)
\approx
p(o_{t+1}\mid s_t,a).
$$

The goal is not maximum context. It is the smallest state for which additional
history would not materially change the next good action.

### 5.2 Tool registry and executor

Each tool needs a contract:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Name and description | help the model select the correct capability |
| Input schema | constrain arguments and enable validation |
| Output schema | make observations predictable |
| Side-effect class | distinguish reads, reversible writes, and irreversible actions |
| Timeout and limits | bound resource use |
| Retry semantics | prevent accidental repeated side effects |
| Permission policy | determine whether execution is allowed or needs approval |

Good tool descriptions say what the tool does, when to use it, and what it does
**not** do. Overlapping tools create selection ambiguity. Huge, raw outputs
consume context and should be normalized or stored as artifacts.

Tools are both **actuators** and **sensors**. An edit, deployment, or message
changes the environment; a search, test, schema inspection, or diagnostic read
primarily reduces uncertainty. A useful epistemic action may have little direct
task reward but high information value:

$$
a^*
=
\arg\max_a
\left[
\mathbb E[V(a)]
+\beta I(o_{t+1};z\mid s_t,a)
\right],
$$

where $z$ is an unknown fact relevant to the decision. This explains why
running a cheap test often beats spending many more tokens predicting whether
the code will work.

### 5.3 State and memory

At least four kinds of state should be distinguished:

- **event log:** append-only record of decisions, calls, observations, and errors
- **working state:** current plan, completed steps, open questions, and budgets
- **artifacts:** files, patches, reports, datasets, logs, and generated outputs
- **long-term memory:** durable knowledge intended for reuse across tasks

Weng highlights the filesystem as an effective persistent-memory substrate for
long-horizon work. Models already understand files, paths, diffs, and shell
operations from pretraining; artifacts remain inspectable outside the context
window and survive interruptions.

Do not confuse persistence with relevance. A file can preserve everything, but
the context compiler must still select what matters now.

For recovery, make the event log **replayable**, not merely readable. Codex
persists append-only JSONL rollouts and reconstructs thread history from stored
items and lifecycle markers. Derived UI state can then be rebuilt after a
disconnect instead of becoming a second, inconsistent source of truth.

### 5.4 Workflow controller

The controller determines the shape of execution:

$$
\text{plan}
\rightarrow
\text{act}
\rightarrow
\text{observe}
\rightarrow
\text{verify}
\rightarrow
\text{revise}.
$$

It owns:

- iteration and termination conditions
- token, time, monetary, and tool-call budgets
- clarification and approval transitions
- retries, fallback tools, and escalation
- background-job and subagent lifecycles
- recovery after interruption

The workflow may be a general loop, a deterministic DAG, or a hybrid in which
code fixes the outer stages and the model makes local decisions.

Name the controller's timescales explicitly. Codex separates a durable
conversation **thread**, a user-facing **turn**, and each model **sampling
step** within that turn. Budgets, cancellation, caches, and persistence may
belong to different levels; a generic “agent step” obscures who owns what.

For uncertain environments, prefer a receding-horizon pattern:

$$
\text{plan}
\rightarrow
\text{act briefly}
\rightarrow
\text{observe}
\rightarrow
\text{replan}.
$$

This resembles model predictive control. A long fixed plan assumes that distant
future states are predictable; short execution bursts allow observations to
correct the plan. The controller should also allocate compute between internal
simulation and acting. When an action is cheap, reversible, and informative,
act-and-observe is often preferable to extended reasoning.

### 5.5 Verifiers

A verifier converts “I think I am done” into observable completion evidence.
Examples include:

- unit tests and static checks for code
- schema validation for structured outputs
- source-entailment checks for research
- row counts and invariants for data pipelines
- screenshots or DOM checks for interfaces
- explicit user confirmation for subjective decisions

Verification should test the artifact or environment state, not merely ask the
same model whether its answer looks correct.

More generally, verifiers perform **surprise engineering**:

$$
\delta_t
=
\operatorname{Compare}
(\text{expected consequence},\text{observed consequence}).
$$

A good environment makes wrong beliefs produce cheap, specific, actionable
observations. Coding agents benefit from unusually dense signals—compiler
errors, test failures, types, linters, and diffs—while research and open-ended
work require more deliberate verifiers for coverage and correctness.

### 5.6 Permission layer

Permissions belong outside the model's editable reasoning loop. The harness
should apply least privilege and classify actions by consequence:

- read-only inspection
- reversible local mutation
- external communication or publication
- financial, destructive, privileged, or difficult-to-reverse action

High-impact actions may require user approval even when the model is confident.
Retrieved documents and tool outputs are untrusted data, not instructions that
can modify the permission policy.

Security is normally a composition rather than one switch. Codex combines OS
sandboxing, approval policy, command rules, managed network policy, and
agent-native telemetry. These controls cover different failure modes. Also note
that sandboxing a built-in shell does not automatically sandbox an external MCP
tool; every capability needs an explicit trust and policy boundary.

Formally, the permission layer enforces

$$
a_t\in\mathcal A_{\text{allowed}}(s_t).
$$

This constrains the states the system can reach. Strong boundaries can enable
greater autonomy inside the safe action set because catastrophic trajectories
are excluded by code rather than discouraged only through prompting.

### 5.7 Observability

A production harness should make trajectories explainable after the fact:

- model and prompt versions
- compiled context metadata
- model decisions and tool calls
- validated arguments and normalized results
- state transitions and artifact versions
- retries, timeouts, approvals, and failures
- token use, latency, and monetary cost
- verifier outcomes and final termination reason

Observability is not only for dashboards. Without it, harness optimization
cannot distinguish a bad model decision from a bad tool description, stale
state, parser bug, permission denial, or verifier failure.

Tracing creates an outer feedback loop around the agent's inner loop:

$$
\underbrace{s_t\rightarrow a_t\rightarrow o_{t+1}\rightarrow s_{t+1}}
_{\text{agent loop}},
\qquad
\underbrace{\text{trajectories}\rightarrow\text{failure analysis}
\rightarrow\text{harness change}\rightarrow\text{new trajectories}}
_{\text{development loop}}.
$$

A final success score says whether a run failed, but the trajectory is needed to
attribute why it failed.

Prefer typed lifecycle events over scraping rendered text. Codex app-server
exposes thread, turn, item, approval, interruption, and completion events so
different clients can project the same core state. This separation makes
reconnection, testing, and protocol compatibility tractable.

## 6. Context Engineering

Context is the model's working memory and control surface. Treat it as a compiled
view of state, not a transcript dump.

A rough selection objective is

$$
\max_{c\subseteq\mathcal I}
\frac{
\operatorname{relevance}(c)
\cdot
\operatorname{reliability}(c)
}{
\operatorname{tokens}(c)
}
$$

subject to mandatory instructions and a context budget.

### Practical hierarchy

Keep these layers distinguishable:

1. **rules:** stable and authoritative
2. **task:** goal, constraints, and definition of done
3. **state:** plan, progress, budgets, and open failures
4. **evidence:** selected observations needed for the next decision
5. **history:** recent interactions useful for local coherence

### Compaction

When context grows:

- keep full artifacts and logs outside the prompt
- summarize completed phases into structured state
- preserve unresolved errors and user constraints verbatim
- retain pointers from summaries to raw evidence
- discard duplicated tool output and obsolete plans
- test whether the compacted state supports resuming after interruption

Lossy compaction is dangerous when it silently drops a constraint, failed
attempt, or source attribution.

## 7. Workflow Design Patterns

Weng identifies three recurring patterns.

### Pattern 1: workflow automation

Define an environment in which the model can execute, test, inspect results,
and iterate. The feedback loop matters more than a single elaborate prompt.

For coding:

```text
inspect repository -> edit -> run tests -> diagnose -> revise -> verify diff
```

For [agentic search](agentic_search.qmd):

```text
decompose -> search -> read -> update evidence gaps -> search again -> verify
```

### Pattern 2: filesystem as persistent memory

Store rich state and artifacts in files while keeping only a compact index in
context. This supports long-running tasks, auditability, recovery, and handoff.

Useful artifacts include:

- `plan.md` for mutable strategy
- machine-readable task state
- experiment configurations and results
- patches and source files
- background-job logs
- evidence ledgers and research summaries
- a concise resumption checkpoint

The names are conventions, not requirements. Avoid creating ceremonial files
that no component actually reads.

### Pattern 3: subagents and background jobs

Parallel work helps when subtasks are independent and expensive enough to
justify coordination. The harness needs process-management operations:

- start with bounded scope and inputs
- assign identifiers and resource budgets
- inspect status and logs
- interrupt or cancel stalled work
- persist outputs as shared artifacts
- merge results and resolve conflicts

Subagents should not exist merely to imitate an organization chart. Every
delegation adds context duplication, synchronization, and error-propagation
cost.

Mechanistically, multi-agent execution is conditional computation, context
partitioning, and sometimes parallel search. It helps when specialists can work
with mostly independent state. If their subtasks depend on heavily shared hidden
context, decomposition can discard information and cost more than one coherent
trajectory.

## 8. A Minimal Harness Skeleton

The following sketch shows the control boundary. It omits provider-specific
types and persistence details.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any, Protocol


@dataclass
class ToolCall:
    name: str
    arguments: dict[str, Any]


@dataclass
class Decision:
    tool_call: ToolCall | None = None
    final_answer: str | None = None


@dataclass
class AgentState:
    goal: str
    events: list[dict[str, Any]] = field(default_factory=list)
    steps: int = 0


class Model(Protocol):
    def decide(self, context: list[dict], tools: list[dict]) -> Decision: ...


class ContextCompiler(Protocol):
    def compile(self, state: AgentState) -> list[dict]: ...


class ToolExecutor(Protocol):
    def schemas(self) -> list[dict]: ...
    def validate_and_run(self, call: ToolCall) -> Any: ...


class Verifier(Protocol):
    def accepts(self, state: AgentState, answer: str) -> bool: ...


def run_agent(model, context, tools, verifier, state, max_steps=30):
    while state.steps < max_steps:
        messages = context.compile(state)
        decision = model.decide(messages, tools.schemas())
        state.steps += 1

        if decision.final_answer is not None:
            if verifier.accepts(state, decision.final_answer):
                return decision.final_answer
            state.events.append({"type": "verification_failed"})
            continue

        if decision.tool_call is None:
            state.events.append({"type": "invalid_decision"})
            continue

        # Authorization, schema validation, timeouts, and retry policy live here.
        try:
            observation = tools.validate_and_run(decision.tool_call)
            state.events.append(
                {
                    "type": "tool_result",
                    "call": decision.tool_call,
                    "observation": observation,
                }
            )
        except Exception as error:
            state.events.append(
                {
                    "type": "tool_error",
                    "call": decision.tool_call,
                    "error": repr(error),
                }
            )

    raise RuntimeError("agent exhausted its step budget")
```

The code's value lies in what it refuses to delegate to the model: validation,
authorization, event recording, hard limits, and the completion check.

## 9. Failure Handling and Recovery

Long-horizon agents should expect partial failure.

| Failure | Harness response |
|---|---|
| malformed tool arguments | reject before execution and return a compact schema error |
| transient network error | bounded retry with backoff and idempotency protection |
| deterministic tool error | expose diagnostic output; do not repeat unchanged calls forever |
| context overflow | compact state and preserve raw artifacts externally |
| repeated action loop | detect repeated call signatures and force replanning or stop |
| background job stalls | poll logs, enforce timeout, then interrupt or escalate |
| verifier fails | attach exact failed condition and resume work |
| authority missing | stop and ask the user rather than inventing permission |
| process interruption | reload durable state and resume from the last consistent checkpoint |

Retries are especially dangerous for non-idempotent tools. Repeating a timed-out
payment, message, or deployment may duplicate the side effect even when the
first response was lost.

### Reflection should follow evidence

Asking the same model to “reflect” without a new observation may provide useful
extra inference, but it does not change the evidence. The stronger loop is

$$
a_t
\rightarrow
o_{t+1}
\rightarrow
\delta_t
\rightarrow
\text{root-cause attribution}
\rightarrow
s_{t+1}.
$$

Reflection should identify which assumption, plan step, tool interpretation, or
completion criterion the observation falsified. Without this attribution, an
agent may respond to a failed test by making unrelated changes or repeating the
same action in different words.

## 10. Designing the Right Amount of Harness

There is a spectrum:

| Style | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Minimal general loop | adapts broadly and benefits directly from stronger models | may wander or miss domain invariants |
| Prompt-heavy scaffold | fast to prototype | brittle, opaque, and difficult to test |
| Deterministic workflow | predictable and easy to observe | inflexible when the path depends on new evidence |
| Hybrid harness | code enforces stages and invariants; model handles judgment | requires careful interface design |
| Multi-agent organization | parallelism and specialized contexts | high coordination and duplication cost |

Prefer the simplest harness that exposes the necessary environment, feedback,
and invariants. Overengineering often compensates for one model's weakness with
rules that become harmful or redundant as models improve.

## 11. Harness Optimization

Harness changes should be treated like changes to any other learned-system
pipeline:

1. collect complete trajectories and verifier outcomes
2. cluster failures by causal mechanism
3. map each failure to a harness component
4. propose the smallest targeted change
5. predict both improvements and possible regressions
6. evaluate on held-in and held-out tasks
7. accept only evidence-supported changes

Useful failure labels follow the closed-loop decomposition: state-estimation,
prediction, planning, tool, verification, permission, and state-update failure.
This provides better credit assignment than treating every unsuccessful
trajectory as a generic model failure.

Possible optimization targets include:

- system instructions and tool descriptions
- tool schemas and implementations
- context selection and compaction
- workflow topology and stopping rules
- memory read/write policies
- subagent configuration
- recovery and verification logic

Always compare against simple baselines. A more elaborate harness may consume
more test-time compute rather than make better decisions.

Harness configuration can also be part of the model's training distribution.
For example, Kimi K3 varies tools, system prompts, context strategies, skills,
memory, and subagent configurations during agentic RL instead of optimizing for
one fixed scaffold. This teaches robustness across runtimes, but does not remove
the need for task-specific environments and verifiers. See
[How SOTA systems train deep research](agentic_search.qmd#sec-deep-research-training)
for the relationship between harness variation, specialist policies, and a
consolidated research/coding/general-agent model.

### Self-improving harnesses

A model can propose edits to its own harness, forming a loop:

$$
h_t
\xrightarrow{\text{run}}
\text{trajectories}
\xrightarrow{\text{diagnose}}
\Delta h
\xrightarrow{\text{evaluate}}
h_{t+1}.
$$

This expands the optimization surface beyond prompts to executable workflows,
tools, memory, and middleware. It also creates a Goodhart problem: an optimizer
may improve the measured score by weakening the verifier, increasing the budget,
leaking test answers, or changing the task.

Keep these surfaces outside the editable loop:

- evaluator and held-out tasks
- permission and security policy
- model identity and resource budget
- audit log and experiment runner
- acceptance and rollback mechanism

Every accepted harness edit should be attributable to evidence from failures
and expressed as a falsifiable prediction.

## 12. Harness Versus Core Intelligence

Some behavior currently implemented in harness code may eventually become a
native model capability. Stronger models need fewer prompt tricks and recover
from tool errors more naturally.

But several responsibilities remain external by nature:

- connecting to the current environment
- enforcing organizational permissions
- owning durable artifacts and state
- applying resource limits
- validating external side effects
- observing and auditing execution

The boundary will move, but it will not disappear. Better models reduce the
need for brittle scaffolding; they do not eliminate the runtime contract.

## 13. Core Insights

1. **A harness converts model capability into system capability.** End-to-end
   performance cannot be attributed to model weights alone.
2. **Context should be compiled from state, not accumulated as a transcript.**
3. **Use models for judgment and code for invariants.**
4. **Artifacts outlive context.** Files and logs make long-horizon work durable,
   inspectable, and resumable.
5. **Verification closes the loop.** A generated answer is only a candidate
   completion.
6. **Permissions must live outside self-modification.** The agent cannot grant
   itself authority.
7. **Observability enables improvement.** If failure cannot be localized, a
   harness edit is guesswork.
8. **The simplest sufficient harness usually generalizes best.** Add structure
   in response to measured failure, not aesthetic preference.
9. **Tools are sensors as well as actuators.** Information-gathering actions can
   be more valuable than premature execution.
10. **Useful reflection begins with surprise.** New external evidence enables
    belief revision; repeated introspection alone does not.
11. **Planning should remain feedback-sensitive.** Plan, act briefly, observe,
    and replan when the environment is uncertain.
12. **Stable context is a performance feature.** Preserve cacheable prefixes and
    order dynamic inputs deterministically.
13. **Protocols should expose lifecycle, not presentation.** Typed events make
    clients replaceable and state recoverable.
14. **Concurrency belongs in tool metadata.** Parallelize calls only when their
    declared effects can safely overlap.

## Interview Questions

- What is the difference between a model, an agent harness, and an agent
  framework?
- Which decisions should be delegated to a model, and which should remain code?
- How would you design an idempotent tool interface?
- What should be stored in context, working state, artifacts, and long-term
  memory?
- Why does a pre-norm-like “always append history” strategy fail for agents?
- What makes a verifier independent enough to be useful?
- When do subagents improve performance rather than add coordination overhead?
- How should a harness recover after a process interruption?
- Which components must remain immutable in a self-improving harness?
- How would you determine whether a gain came from the harness or additional
  test-time compute?
- Why are tools both actuators and sensors? Give an example of an epistemic tool
  action.
- What makes a verifier produce useful surprise rather than merely another
  model opinion?
- When is receding-horizon planning preferable to committing to a complete
  plan?
- Why is reflection after a failed test more useful than reflection with no new
  evidence?
- Why can two semantically equivalent prompts have different inference costs?
- Why should thread, turn, and sampling-step state be distinguished?
- Why does sandboxing the shell not automatically sandbox every external tool?

## Exercises

- [ ] Implement the minimal loop with one read-only tool and a step budget.
- [ ] Add schema validation, timeouts, and repeated-call detection.
- [ ] Persist event logs and resumable state to files.
- [ ] Design a context compiler that retains unresolved errors while compacting
  completed work.
- [ ] Add a verifier whose result cannot be overwritten by the agent.
- [ ] Classify tools by side-effect risk and design approval policies.
- [ ] Compare a minimal loop with a deterministic workflow on the same tasks.
- [ ] Cluster failed trajectories and propose one falsifiable harness change.
